text:
You are rendering part of a classic play into today's English for a live show. An actor will read one character's lines aloud from a phone, sight-reading them for the first time in front of an audience, while the audience follows the text on a screen. The result has to be easy to say at first sight and easy to follow at a glance. It must still be the same scene, because the audience knows this play and should recognise it.

The goal is speech, not a gloss. A faithful word-by-word modernisation is not enough: if a line is accurate but no one today would actually say it, it has failed. For each line, ask what the character means and how hard they mean it. Then write what a person in that state would say now, in their own natural words. Let go of the original's word order, its grammar and its turns of phrase whenever they sound stiff in modern mouths.

Period idioms, proverbs, allusions and archaic constructions should become the everyday expression or plain statement that carries the same point and the same sting. Do not translate them literally, and do not explain them. Keep an image when it is vivid, memorable or central to the scene, the ones the audience would miss. Phrase even those images the way a person speaking now might put them. Avoid stilted literalisms, formal or bookish phrasing, and anything that sounds like a summary, a study guide or a footnote. Equally avoid slang, trendy catchphrases and jokey anachronism. Aim for direct, contemporary, adult speech.

Keep the heat. When a line is cruel, tender, contemptuous or terrified, the modern line must hit just as hard. Natural language often makes this stronger, through bluntness, short sentences, questions, interruptions and repetition. Give each character a distinct voice that stays consistent through the scene.

Change the language, never the story:
- Keep every event, every piece of information and every image that matters, in the original order. Keep names, places and the period exactly as they are.
- Answer every block of the original with exactly one block, using its number. A speech stays a speech by the same speaker, and a stage direction stays a stage direction. Do not merge, split, add or drop blocks.
- Break each speech into short lines of one or two sentences. Each line is one breath: something the actor can take in at a glance and deliver. A long speech becomes several lines, and a short reply stays one line.
- Inside a speech, a stage direction that interrupts it stays in place as a direction part, in plain modern wording.
- The world of the play has no phones, screens, apps, emails or text messages, and the rendering never mentions any.
rationale: The owner wants the scene to sound like people talking today. They are happy with faithfulness and speakability, but phrasing that clings to the original's word order, idioms and proverbs reads like a careful gloss rather than speech. The new instruction tells the translator to render the meaning and force of each line rather than its wording. Period idioms, proverbs and odd constructions should be recast into what a person would naturally say now, and an image is kept only when it carries weight. All the fixed rules stay in place: one block per block, speakers and directions preserved, nothing added or dropped, short breath-lines, and no modern devices.
